$\begin{aligned}$& $\text{ (a) Density }(\rho)=\frac{\operatorname{Mass}(\mathrm{m})}{\operatorname{Volume}(\mathrm{V})}$\\
& $\mathrm{m}=\rho \mathrm{V} .

$\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}=\rho_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{B}}$ Mass of liquid $C$,

$\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{C}}=\rho_{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{C}}$ Since the mass of liquid is same and the vessels are identical so their area will also same.

Hence from $\mathrm{Eq}^{\mathrm{n}} 1, 2 and 3:

\begin{aligned}$& $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{C}}=\mathrm{M}$\\
& \rho_{$\mathrm{A} }\mathrm{Ah}_{\mathrm{A}}=\rho_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{Ah}_{\mathrm{B}}=\rho_{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{Ah}_{\mathrm{C}}=\mathrm{M}
\end{aligned}$ The product of $\rho and h$ is constant thus if $\rho_A > \rho_B > \rho_C$ then $\mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{A}$} <  $\mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{B}$} <  $\mathrm{h}_{\mathrm{C}$}$.

Hence, the pressure at the bottom will be same.$

[Note that the coefficient of viscosity of air is $1. 8 \times {10}^{- 5}Nm^{- 2}$, density of water is $1000Kgm^{- 3}$. Use $g = 10ms^{- 2}$ and density of air can be neglected in comparison with density of water]
questions.solution:
Terminal velocity is a steady speed achieved by an object freely falling through a viscous gas or liquid. At terminal velocity, the viscous force on the object is equal to the weight of the object minus the buoyance force.

The density of air can be assumed negligible.

$v = \dfrac{2r^{2}\left({ρ}_{S} - {ρ}_{L}\right)g}{9η} ⇒ v = \dfrac{2 \times \left(2 \times {10}^{- 5}\right)^{2} \times \left(1000\right) \times 10}{9 \times 1. 8 \times {10}^{- 5}} ⇒ v = 4. 9 \times {10}^{- 2}ms^{- 1} = 4. 9cms^{- 1}$

$\left(\text{area of orifice}\right) \times \left(\text{velocity of efflux}\right)$

$⇒ 3 . 08 \times {10}^{- 5} = \left(\dfrac{\pid^{2}}{4}\right) \times 20 ⇒ d = \sqrt{\dfrac{4 \times 3 . 08 \times {10}^{- 5}}{\pi \times 20}} = 1 . 4mm$

Density of the material, $\rho=3 \mathrm{ g} / \mathrm{cc}$
Density of the fluid, $\sigma=7 \mathrm{ g} / \mathrm{cc}$
Let the volume of the material be $V and n$ portion of the volume of the block submerged in the fluid.
$\therefore$ Weight of the fluid is $V \rho g$ and weight of the submerged part is $n V \sigma g$

questions.q:
Consider a fluid in a container. Let the density of the fluid at the surface and at depth $H$~be ${ρ}_{0} and ρ$ respectively. The bulk modulus of the fluid is ${B}_{0} .$~If $ρ = \dfrac{ρ0}{1 + \alpha{ρ}_{0}gH}$ then the constant $\alpha$ is
$\left(Assume\dfrac{ρ - {ρ}_{0}}{ρ0} ≪ 1\right)$
questions.solution:
Consider a volume ${V}_{1}$ of liquid at top surface, then due to pressure at depth, same volume becomes& ${V}_{2}$ at depth& $H$.

From the conservation of mass, we have
${ρ}_{0}{V}_{1} = ρ{V}_{2}$
$⇒ ρ = {ρ}_{0} $\$left(\dfrac{V1}{V2}\right) . . .\left(1\right)$

At the below height $H$, extra pressure is given by, $P = ρgH$
From Hooke's law, we have
$P = - $\$beta\dfrac{∆ V}{V1}$
$⇒ P = \beta\left({V}_{1} - {V}_{2}\right){V}_{1}
$⇒ ρgH = $\beta \left({V}_{1} - {V}_{2}\right){V}_{1}$
$⇒ ρgH = \beta \left(1 - \dfrac{V2}{V1}\right)
$⇒ $\dfrac{ρgH}{β} =\left(1 - \dfrac{V2}{V1}\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{V2}{V1} = 1 - \dfrac{ρgH}{β}$
$⇒ \dfrac{V1}{V2} = \dfrac{1}{1 - \dfrac{ρgH}{β}}$
Putting this in equation $\left(1\right)$, we have
$⇒ ρ = {ρ}_{0} \left(\dfrac{1}{1 - \dfrac{ρgH}{β}}\right)
$⇒ ρ = $\dfrac{ρ0}{1 + \left(\left(- \dfrac{1}{β}\right)ρgH\right)}$$
On comparing above relation with given relation, we have
$\alpha = - $\dfrac{1}{β}$

questions.q: Liquid $A$ rises to a height of $10$ cm in a capillary tube and liquid $B$ falls to a depth of $2$ cm in the same tube. The density of $A$ and $B$ are $1g / {cm}^{3}$ and $10g / {cm}^{3}$ respectively. The contact angle of $A$ and $B$ with the tube is $0 °$ and $135 °$ respectively. If the surface tension of $A$ and $B$ are ${S}_{A}$ and ${S}_{B}$ then the ratio $\dfrac{SB}{SA}$ is
questions.solution:
Expression of capillary rise is given by,& $h = \dfrac{4scos\left(\theta\right)}{dρg}$
For~$A$, expression is,~${h}_{A} = \dfrac{4{s}_{A}cos\left(0 °\right)}{{d}_{A} \times {ρ}_{A} \times g}$
$⇒ 10 = \dfrac{4{s}_{A} \times 1}{{d}_{A} \times 1 \times g} . . . \left(1\right)
For~$B$, expression is,~${h}_{B} = $\dfrac{4{s}_{B}cos\left(135 °\right)}{{d}_{B} \times {ρ}_{B} \times g}
$⇒ - 2 = $\dfrac{4{s}_{B}\left(- \dfrac{1}{2}\right)}{{d}_{B} \times 10 \times g}
$⇒ 2 = $\dfrac{4{s}_{B}}{\sqrt{2} \times {d}_{B} \times 10 \times g} . . .\left(2\right)$
On dividing~$\left(2\right)$~by& $\left(1\right)$,
$⇒ \dfrac{2}{10} = \dfrac{4{s}_{B}\sqrt{2} \times {d}_{B} \times 10 \times g}{4{s}_{A} \times 1{d}_{A} \times 1 \times g}$
$⇒ \dfrac{2}{10} = \dfrac{sB}{10\sqrt{2}{s}_{A}}$
$⇒ \dfrac{sB}{sA} = 2\sqrt{2}$

Hooke's law is a law of physics that states that the force needed to extend or compress a spring by some distance scales linearly with respect to that distance—that is, ${F}_{s} = kx$, where $k$ is a constant factor characteristic of the spring, and $x$ is small compared to the total possible deformation of the spring.

questions.solution:
Radius of meniscus, $R=1 \mathrm{ cm}=10^{-2} \mathrm{ m}$
Number of smaller droplets, $n=10^6$
Surface tension, $T=435 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{Nm}^{-1}$
Work done in splitting a large drop of radius $R in n$ smaller drops is
$W=T \times \Delta A$
where, $\Delta A=$ increase in area and $T=$ surface tension.
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad W & =\left(4 \pi R^2\right) T \cdot\left(n^{1 / 3}-1\right) \\
& =4 \times \pi \times\left(1 \times 10^{-2}\right)^2 \times 435 \times 10^{-3} \times\left(\left(10^6\right)^{1 / 3}-1\right) \\
& =54.1 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{ J}
\end{aligned}$

Consider a steady flow of oil in a pipeline. The cross-sectional radius of the pipeline decreases gradually as $r=r_0 e^{-\alpha x}$, where $\alpha=\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$ and x is the distance from the pipeline inlet. If $R_1$ is the Reynold's number
for a certain pipeline cross-section at a distance $x_1$ metre from the inlet and $R_2$ is for distance $\left(x_1+3\right)$ metre, then the ratio $\frac{R_1}{R_2}$ is
questions.solution: Reynold's number of flow is given by $R_e=\frac{2 v \rho r}{\eta}$ where, $v=$ velocity of flow, $\rho=$ density of fluid, $r=$ radius of tube and $\eta=$ viscosity of flow Now, required ratio is $\begin{aligned} & \frac{R_1}{R_2}=\left(\frac{2 v_1 \rho r_1}{\eta}\right) /\left(\frac{2 v_2 \rho r_2}{\eta}\right) \\ & \frac{R_1}{R_2}=\frac{v_1}{v_2} \times \frac{r_1}{r_2}\end{aligned}$ From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\begin{aligned} \frac{R_1}{R_2} & =\frac{r_2^2}{r_1^2} \times \frac{r_1}{r_2}=\frac{r_2}{r_1} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \frac{R_1}{R_2} & =\frac{r_0 e^{-\alpha\left(x_1+3\right)}}{r_0 e^{-\alpha x_1}}=\frac{e^{-\alpha x_1} \cdot e^{-3 \alpha}}{e^{-\alpha x_1}}=e^{-3 \alpha} \\ & =\frac{1}{e^{3 \alpha}}=\frac{1}{e} \quad\left(\because \alpha=\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{ m}^{-1}\right)\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A copper wire of cross-sectional area $0. 01{cm}^{2}$ is under a tension of $22N$. Find the percentage change in the cross-sectional area (Young's modulus of copper $= 1. 1 \times {10}^{11}Nm^{- 2}$ and Poisson ratio$= 0. 32$ )
questions.solution:
Given,

The area of cross-section of copper wire is $A = 0. 01{cm}^{2}$

Tension in the wire is $T = 22N$

Young's modulus of copper wire is $Y = 1. 1 \times {10}^{11}Nm^{- 2}$

Poisson ratio is $\sigma = 0. 32$

Using the formula of Young's modulus of wire,

$Y = \dfrac{F}{A} \times \dfrac{l}{dl}$

The longitudinal strain is given by,

$⇒ \dfrac{dl}{l} = \dfrac{T}{AY}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dl}{l} = \dfrac{22}{{10}^{- 6} \times 1. 1 \times {10}^{11}} = 20 \times {10}^{- 5}$

The Poisson ratio of wire is given by,

$\sigma = \dfrac{\dfrac{dr}{r}}{\dfrac{dl}{l}}$

The lateral strain in the wire is given by

$⇒ \dfrac{dr}{r} = \sigma \times \dfrac{dl}{l} = 0. 32 \times 20 \times {10}^{- 5} = 6. 4 \times {10}^{- 5}$

The percentage change in area is given by

$⇒ \dfrac{dA}{A} \times 100 = \dfrac{2dr}{r} \times 100 = 2 \times 6. 4 \times {10}^{- 3}$

Applying the Bernoulli equation,

${p}_{1} + \dfrac{1}{2}ρ{v}_{1}^{2} + ρg{h}_{1} = {p}_{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}ρ{v}_{2}^{2} + ρg{h}_{2}$

Here, the height of the water in the tank is ${h}_{1}$,

${p}_{1}$ is the pressure of water in the tank, and

${v}_{1}$ is the velocity of the water.&

${h}_{2}$ is the hole's height,

${p}_{2}$ is the pressure at hole, and

${v}_{2}$ is the water's pace at the hole and

$ρ$ represents& the water density.

There acts the same atmospheric& pressure at the top of the tank and at the hole, thus ${p}_{1} = {p}_{2}$.

We will neglect the water velocity at the top since the tank is large as its velocity is much smaller than the velocity at the hole.

Now, the Bernoulli equation becomes, $ρg{h}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{2}ρ{v}_{2}^{2} + ρg{h}_{2}$

$⇒ {v}_{2} = \sqrt{2g\left({h}_{1} - {h}_{2}\right)}$

$⇒ {v}_{2} = \sqrt{2 \times 9. 81 \times \left(0. 2\right)} = 1. 98ms^{- 1}$

The drainage rate is ${A}_{2}{v}_{2} = 6 \times {10}^{- 4} \times 1. 98$

$⇒ {A}_{2}{v}_{2} = 1. 18 \times {10}^{- 3} = 1. 2 \times {10}^{- 3}m^{3}s^{- 1}$

questions.q: Two spherical soap bubbles of radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ in vacuum combine under isothermal conditions. The resulting bubble has a radius equal to:
questions.solution:
Excess of pressure, inside the first bubble
$p_1=\frac{4 T}{r_1}$
Similarly, $\quad p_2=\frac{4 T}{r_2}$
Let the radius of the large bubble be $R$.
Then, excess of pressure inside the large bubble,
$p=\frac{4 T}{R}$
Under isothermal condition, temperature remains constant.
So, $\quad P V=p_1 V_1+p_2 V_2\frac{4 T}{R}\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3\right)=\frac{4 T}{r_1}\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi r_1^3\right)+\frac{4 T}{r_2}\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi r_2^3\right)R^2=r_1^2+r_2^2\Rightarrow \quad R=\sqrt{r_1^2+r_2^2}$

questions.q:
The rate of steady volume flow of water through a capillary tube of length $l$ and radius $r$, under a pressure difference of $p$ is $V$. This tube is connected with another tube of the same length but half the radius, in series. Then, the rate of steady volume flow through them is
(The pressure difference across the combination is $p$. )
questions.solution:
The rate of flow of water inside a capillary, $V=\frac{\pi p r^4}{8 n l^{\prime}}$
Pressure difference, $p=\frac{V(8 n l)}{\pi r^4}$
In series combination,
$p=p_1+p_2$
where, $p_1 and p_2$ are the pressure difference in the two tubes.
$\therefore \quad \frac{V(8 n l)}{\pi r^4}=\frac{V^{\prime}(8 n l)}{\pi r^4}+\frac{V^{\prime}(8 n l)}{\pi(r / 2)^4}$
In series combination, rate of flow of water $\left(V^{\prime}\right)$ will be same in both the tubes.
$\therefore \quad \frac{V}{r^4}=\frac{V^{\prime}}{r^4}+\frac{V^{\prime} \times 16}{r^4}V=V^{\prime}+16 V^{\prime}V^{\prime}=\frac{V}{17}$

Time taken, $t=\sqrt{\frac{2 h}{g}}$
Time taken for the level of water to fall from $h$ to $h / 2$ to 0 ,
$t_1=\sqrt{\frac{2}{g}}\left(\sqrt{h_1}-\sqrt{h_2}\right)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{g}} \left(\sqrt{h}-\sqrt{\frac{h}{2}}\right)=\sqrt{\frac{2 h}{g}}\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)
Similarly, time taken for the level of water to fall from $ h / 2$ to 0 .
$t_2=$\sqrt{\frac{2}{g}}\left(\sqrt{\frac{h}{2}}-0\right)\Rightarrow \quad t_2=\sqrt{\frac{2 h}{g}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\therefore \quad \frac{t_1}{t_2}=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{2 h}{g}}\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}{\sqrt{\frac{2 h}{g}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}=\frac{\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}-1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}{1 / \sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}-1$

questions.q:
A mercury drop of radius $1 \mathrm{ cm}$ is sprayed into $10^6$ drops of equal size. The energy expended in joules is
(Surface tension of mercury is $460 \times 10^{-3}\mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m})$
questions.solution:
$R=1 \mathrm{ cm}, n=10^6$
Total volume of small drops = volume of big drop
$\begin{aligned} 10^6 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 & =\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \\ 10^6 r^3 & =R^3 \\ r & =\frac{R}{10^2}\end{aligned}$
Energy expended $=$ work done
$\begin{aligned} & =\Delta A \times T \\ & =\left(n 4 \pi r^2-4 \pi R^2\right) T \\ & =4 \pi\left(n r^2-R^2\right) T \\ & =4 \pi\left(n\left(\frac{R}{10^2}\right)^2-R^2\right) T \\ & =4 \pi R^2\left[n \frac{1}{10^4}-1\right] T \\ & =4 \times 3.14 \times\left(1 \times 10^{-2}\right)^2 \\ & \quad \times\left[10^6 \times \frac{1}{10^4}-1\right] \times 460 \times 10^{-3} \\ & =4 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-4} \times\left(10^2-1\right) \times 460 \times 10^{-3} \\ & =4 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-4} \times 99 \times 460 \times 10^{-3} \\ & =0.057 \mathrm{ J}\end{aligned}$

Rate of flow of water
$\begin{aligned} & Q=2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{ m}^3 / \mathrm{s} \\ & Q=\frac{\pi P r^2}{8 \eta l}\end{aligned}\Rightarrow \quad P=\frac{Q(8 \eta l)}{\pi r^4}\eta=$ coefficient of viscosity of water $=10^{-3}$ SI units
$\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad P & =\frac{2 \times 10^{-3} \times 8 \times 10^{-3} \times 3140}{3.14 \times\left(4 \times 10^{-2}\right)^4} \\ & =\frac{2 \times 8 \times 3140 \times 10^{-6}}{3.14 \times 256 \times 10^{-8}} \\ & =\frac{3140 \times 10^2}{3.14 \times 16} \\ & \left.=\frac{100 \times 10^3}{16}\right] \\ & =6.25 \times 10^3 \mathrm{ N} / \mathrm{m}^2\end{aligned}$
